slides.text: The lecture is titled "Convolutional Architectures and Beyond".
The lecture is presented by Sergey Nikolenko.
The lecture is at Harbour Space University.
The lecture date is June 16, 2026.
LaMarcus Thompson's Switchback Railway opened at Coney Island on June 16, 1884.
The Switchback Railway was the first purpose-built roller coaster.
The Switchback Railway ambled along at about six miles per hour.
A ride on the Switchback Railway cost a nickel.
The Switchback Railway proved profitable enough to spawn an entire industry.
On June 16, 1904, James Joyce set the whole action of Ulysses on that date.
Ulysses has over seven hundred pages.
The action of Ulysses is set on an ordinary Dublin day.
James Joyce chose June 16, 1904 because it was the date of his first walk with Nora Barnacle.
Readers now retrace the events of Ulysses each Bloomsday in Edwardian dress.
On June 16, 1911, the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company was incorporated in New York.
The company merged a scale maker, a time-clock maker, and Herman Hollerith's census tabulating-machine business.
The conglomerate was not renamed IBM until 1924.
On June 16, 1960, Alfred Hitchcock's Psycho premiered in New York.
The premiere had a strict "no one admitted after the start" rule.
The rule was enforced by Pinkerton guards and life-sized cardboard cutouts of the director.
That gimmick is the reason why films have had fixed start times ever since.
On June 16, 1963, Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space.
She was a textile worker and amateur parachutist.
She was aboard Vostok 6.
She circled the Earth 48 times in just under three days.
No other woman would reach orbit for another 19 years.
There is a huge number of different models based on the CNN idea.
Most CNN-based models are accompanied by code.
Many CNN-based models provide models pretrained on the ImageNet or other large standard datasets.
These models are usually all based on a few standard ideas.
In this lecture, we are going to consider those standard ideas.
The VGG (Oxford Visual Geometry Group) approach represents large convolutions as compositions of 3x3 convolutions.
Representing large convolutions as compositions of 3x3 convolutions reduces the number of weights and makes the network deeper.
The VGG network was used in the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Competition (ILSVRC-2014).
NVIDIA has been optimizing GPUs especially for 3x3 convolutions.
Inception and GoogLeNet are based on the "network in network" idea.
The "network in network" idea is used to reduce the number of weights even further.
Another idea in Inception/GoogLeNet is to use additional classifiers, which are additional terms for the objective function.
In Inception v2 (Szegedy et al., 2015), n×n convolutions were replaced by n×1 and 1×n convolutions.
Filter banks in Inception v2 became wide rather than deep.
The same paper (Szegedy et al., 2015) introduced Inception v3.
Inception v3 uses RMSProp, factorized 7x7 convolutions, and batchnorm in additional classifiers.
In a regular classifier, the softmax is trained with a hard objective q(k) = [k=y].
In the hard objective, the arguments of the softmax function "want" to grow unboundedly.
As a result, the models overfit and become too certain.
A possible solution is label smoothing.
In label smoothing, we optimize q'(k) = (1 - ε)[k=y] + ε u(k) for some prior distribution u(k).
An example prior distribution is u(k) = 1/K.
Residual learning involves training the differences (residues) between one layer and the next.
In residual learning, the gradients will be able to flow with no obstacle.
A function implemented by a residual unit is y(k) = F(x(k)) + x(k).
In the residual unit, x(k) is the input vector of layer k.
F(x) is the function computed by the layer.
y(k) is the output of the residual layer and will become x(k+1) for the next layer.
The gradient of y(k) with respect to x(k) is ∂y(k)/∂x(k) = 1 + ∂F(x(k))/∂x(k).
When F becomes saturated, the gradient does not vanish because of the identity term.
Residual learning has allowed for very deep networks.
Another similar approach is highway networks by Jürgen Schmidhuber.
In highway networks, y(k) is represented as C(x(k))x(k) + T(x(k))F(x(k)).
C is the carry gate.
T is the transform gate.
Usually it is a convex combination, with C = 1 - T.
Practice shows that the residual connections should be as "straight" as possible.
ResNeXt, introduced by Xie et al. in 2016, replaces ResNet units with "split-transform-merge" units.
These units are similar to Inception units.
In ResNeXt, the input is divided into blocks with respect to channels, and each block gets its own convolutions.
The idea in ResNeXt is similar to group convolutions.
Group convolutions were used already in AlexNet for parallelization.
ResNeXt units yield a kind of specialization in the results.
Another classic paper by Szegedy et al. in 2016 introduced Inception v4 and Inception ResNet.
Inception v4 standardizes everything and simplifies the units.
Inception v4 has a "stem" component first.
Inception v4 has three basic blocks named A, B, and C.
Inception v4 has special reduction blocks to reduce the dimensions.
Inception ResNet adds residual connections to the blocks of Inception v4.
Inception ResNet has no pooling but still has reduction blocks.
The architectures of Inception v4 and Inception ResNet have become even simpler.
There is an Inception ResNet v2.
The Inception v4 and Inception ResNet architectures work quite well.
SqueezeNet, introduced by Iandola et al. in 2017, is a method to reduce the number of parameters.
One technique in SqueezeNet is to replace 3x3 filters with 1x1 filters.
Another technique is to reduce the number of inputs for 3x3 convolutions.
Another technique is to delay downsampling as late as possible to increase the size of activation maps.
SqueezeNet uses a Fire module.
The Fire module consists of a squeeze convolutional layer with only 1x1 convolutions.
The Fire module also has an expand layer with 1x1 and 3x3 convolutions.
SqueezeNet has a general architecture.
SqueezeNet achieves 50 times fewer parameters than AlexNet.
MobileNet, introduced by Howard et al. in 2017, is a network designed for mobile devices.
MobileNet uses depthwise separable convolutions.
Depthwise separable convolutions decompose a convolution into a depthwise convolution and a 1x1 convolution.
In depthwise separable convolutions, the depthwise convolution has one filter for each channel.
With depthwise separable convolutions, the structure of a layer becomes more complex.
However, it has fewer weights.
The overall MobileNet architecture is not very deep.
MobileNet can save a lot of parameters.
This comes at the price of a small decrease in quality.
EfficientNet was introduced by Tan and Le in 2019.
EfficientNet uses neural architecture search.
The goal of EfficientNet is to design state-of-the-art networks at a fraction of the cost.
EfficientNet involves different kinds of scaling for the models.
An important problem in deep neural networks is internal covariate shift.
Internal covariate shift occurs because when the weights of a layer change, the distribution of its outputs changes.
Due to the changed output distribution, the next layer has to re-train almost from scratch, as it did not expect these outputs.
Moreover, neurons in the next layer might have already reached saturation, making quick re-training impossible.
Internal covariate shift seriously impedes learning.
A characteristic example demonstrates that the distributions in internal covariate shift are very different.
One attempt to address internal covariate shift is to normalize (whiten) after every layer.
This approach does not work.
Consider a layer that simply adds a bias b to its inputs u, and then normalizes: ˆx = x - E[x], where x = u + b.
On the next gradient descent step, b is updated to b+Δb.
However, ˆx does not change because u + b + Δb - E[u + b + Δb] = u + b - E[u + b].
As a result, the biases will simply increase unboundedly, and the training will not progress.
This is not a good outcome.
Another approach is to add normalization as a layer: ˆx = Norm(x, X).
This approach requires the entire dataset X.
In gradient descent, one would need to compute the partial derivatives ∂Norm/∂x and ∂Norm/∂X.
Additionally, one would need to compute the covariance matrix Cov[x] = E[xx^T] - E[x]E[x]^T.
This approach definitely does not work.
The solution to the normalization problem is batch normalization.
In batch normalization, each component is normalized separately over the current mini-batch, not over the whole dataset.
After batch normalization, we have ˆxk = (xk - E[xk]) / sqrt(Var[xk]).
The statistics E[xk] and Var[xk] are computed over the current mini-batch.
One problem with batch normalization is that nonlinearities disappear.
For example, after batch normalization, we almost always get into the region where the activation function σ is very close to linear.
To fix the disappearance of nonlinearities in batch normalization, we must allow the batchnorm layer enough flexibility to sometimes do nothing with the inputs.
This is achieved by introducing additional shift and scale parameters γk and βk.
The batch normalization transformation becomes yk = γk ˆxk + βk.
γk and βk are new variables that are trained just like the weights.
There is a final scheme for batch normalization.
The original idea behind batch normalization was to reduce internal covariate shift.
It turned out that batch normalization's effectiveness does not really depend on reducing internal covariate shift.
Batch normalization helps with regularization.
Batch normalization makes dropout unnecessary.
One possible reason is that batch normalization smooths the gradients, reducing the Lipschitz constant (Santurkar et al., 2019).
Another reason is that batch normalization decouples the learning of the direction and the length of the weight vectors, which improves training.
There are results showing that batch normalization helps achieve linear convergence in ordinary gradient descent.
Mini-batch normalization has become essentially the standard normalization method.
The idea of normalization has evolved further.
Laurent et al. (2016) found that batch normalization does not help recurrent networks.
Cooijmans et al. (2016) introduced recurrent batch normalization.
Salimans and Kingma (2016) introduced weight normalization to improve training.
In weight normalization, the weights are used as h_i = f( γ/||w_i|| w_i^T x + b_i ).
Weight normalization rescales the gradient, stabilizes its norm, and brings the gradient's covariance matrix closer to the identity, which improves training.
The lecture aims to make sense of the landscape of normalization methods.
In general, all normalization methods use the same operations.
The normalization methods differ in the set of operations and in the dimensions they are applied over.
Batch normalization is applied over the mini-batch dimension and is often used for images.
Layer normalization is applied over the channels and spatial dimensions, i.e., over all outputs of a layer.
Layer normalization is used mostly for vectors, in particular in transformers.
Instance normalization is applied only over the spatial dimensions, dropping the channels.
Instance normalization is used, for example, in AdaIN for style transfer.
Group normalization splits the channels into groups.
Weight standardization standardizes the weights rather than the activations.
Weight standardization does this separately for each channel.
Weight standardization also normalizes the gradients during backpropagation.
Group normalization combined with weight standardization was used in BiT (Big Transfer).
The slide presents a summary of normalization methods.
In general, the study of variants is a big science (Huang et al., 2020).
The science of variants is really big.
Sequences include financial time series, language, and sound.
There are different kinds of sequence-based problems.
To apply a neural network to a sequence-based problem, one approach is to use a sliding window.
For sequence-based problems, it would be better to have a hidden state and update it.
The whole idea of recurrent neural networks (RNN) is to have a hidden state and update it.
The state update equation s_i = h(x_i, x_{i+1}, x_{i+2}, s_{i-1}) creates cycles in the computational graph.
The computational graph of an RNN can be unrolled, for example y_6 = f(x_3, x_4, x_5, h(x_2, x_3, x_4, h(x_1, x_2, x_3, s_0))).
Formally, there is no problem with backpropagation because the graph can be unrolled.
Practically, unrolled RNNs are very deep networks with many shared weights, causing many issues.
In a simple RNN, the formal equations are: a_t = b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t, s_t = f(a_t), o_t = c + V s_t, y_t = h(o_t).
f is the recurrent nonlinearity.
h is the output function.
Simple RNNs have two problems: exploding gradients and vanishing gradients.
In RNNs, because we multiply by the same matrix W repeatedly, the norm of the gradient grows or decreases exponentially.
When the gradient norm grows exponentially, this is the exploding gradient problem.
Exploding gradients can be handled by bounding the gradients from above.
There are two versions of gradient clipping: bounding the norm or bounding every value.
In Keras, gradient norm clipping can be implemented with optimizers.SGD(lr=0.01, clipnorm=1.).
Alternatively, gradient value clipping can be implemented with optimizers.SGD(lr=0.01, clipvalue=.05).
RNNs have bifurcation points, which explain gaps in the loss surface.
For some sequence-processing tasks, context from both directions is needed.
In a bidirectional RNN, the forward state is s_t = \sigma(b + W s_{t-1} + U x_t).
The backward state is s'_t = \sigma(b' + W' s'_{t+1} + U' x_t).
The output is o_t = c + V s_t + V' s'_t.
The final output is y_t = h(o_t).
The concept of bidirectional RNN generalizes to other constructions.
In vanilla RNNs, the vanishing gradient problem arises because we have to multiply by W at each time step.
Vanishing gradients make it impossible for RNNs to have long-term memory.
The basic idea from ResNet is to provide a "constant error carousel", which is a shortcut for gradients.
The idea for LSTM originated in the mid-1990s by Schmidhuber: to construct RNNs from a more complex unit that has a gradient shortcut and explicit memory control.
LSTM stands for long short-term memory.
In a vanilla LSTM, c_t is the cell state and h_t is the hidden state.
The input gate and forget gate control whether the cell state c_t is changed to the new candidate cell state.
The candidate cell state is c'_t = \tanh(W_{xc} x_t + W_{hc} h_{t-1} + b_{c'}).
The input gate is i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate is f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate is o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + b_o).
The cell state update is c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t.
The hidden state is h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t).
The LSTM cell controls the cell state using the hidden state and weights.
When the forget gate is closed (f_t = 1), the cell state update becomes c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot c'_t, so the partial derivative \partial c_t/\partial c_{t-1} = 1.
This identity derivative provides the constant error carousel.
LSTM was developed in the mid-1990s by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, with papers in 1995 and 1997.
The modern form of LSTM was completed by Gers and Schmidhuber in 2000.
A problem with the early LSTM is that the gates do not have access to the cell state c; they only see h_{t-1} = o_{t-1} \odot \tanh(c_{t-1}).
If the output gate is closed, the behavior of LSTM does not depend on the cell state at all.
This lack of dependence is undesirable.
To address the problem, peepholes (additional weight matrices) are added.
With peepholes, the input gate becomes i_t = \sigma(W_{xi} x_t + W_{hi} h_{t-1} + W_{pi} c_{t-1} + b_i).
The forget gate becomes f_t = \sigma(W_{xf} x_t + W_{hf} h_{t-1} + W_{pf} c_{t-1} + b_f).
The output gate becomes o_t = \sigma(W_{xo} x_t + W_{ho} h_{t-1} + W_{po} c_{t-1} + b_o).
There are many LSTM variations, allowing removal or addition of gates, peepholes, and activation functions.
The question of how to choose among these variations arises.
The paper "LSTM: a Search Space Odyssey" by Greff et al. (2015) provides an experimental comparison of many LSTM variations.
Some significantly simpler architectures, including ones with one less gate, performed comparably to the vanilla LSTM.
Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) were developed by Cho et al. in 2014.
GRU implements the constant error carousel and is simpler than LSTM.
The GRU update gate is u_t = \sigma(W_{xu} x_t + W_{hu} h_{t-1} + b_u).
The reset gate is r_t = \sigma(W_{xr} x_t + W_{hr} h_{t-1} + b_r).
The candidate hidden state is h'_t = \tanh(W_{xh'} x_t + W_{hh'} (r_t \odot h_{t-1})).
The hidden state update is h_t = (1 - u_t) \odot h'_t + u_t \odot h_{t-1}.
GRU does not distinguish between cell state and hidden state.
GRU uses fewer weight matrices (6) compared to LSTM (8 or 11 with peepholes).
GRU has only very slightly worse performance than LSTM.
Due to its simplicity, more GRU units can be used within a given computational budget, potentially leading to better networks.
There are additional variations beyond GRU.
Józefowicz, Zaremba, and Sutskever (2015) conducted a large experimental comparison of RNN architectures using an evolutionary approach.
This study identified three interesting architectures.

Technically, the most interesting aspects of AlexNet are two things.
AlexNet is a pretty standard convolutional architecture.
AlexNet is split in two.
That split was the first actual industrial-scale instance of model parallelization.
In deep learning, you have huge models and huge data sets, so you need to parallelize and make use of multiple GPUs if available.
There are two main ways to parallelize: data parallelization and model parallelization.

Data parallelization involves having one mini-batch in GPU 1, another in GPU 2, another in GPU 3, running them in parallel, collecting the results, and doing a single update based on weight updates from all GPUs.
With data parallelization, you don't have to change anything in your implementation; the network works as usual.
The only difference is that with multiple GPUs in parallel, you are effectively increasing the mini-batch size by splitting the mini-batch across GPUs.
There is a lot of work on data parallelization because it can be done in many smart and interesting ways, but the basic idea is simple.
Model parallelization is more complicated.
In model parallelization, the assumption is that the model does not fit on a single GPU.
If the model does not fit on a single GPU, you need to put half of the model on one GPU and the other half on another GPU.
AlexNet was doing model parallelization already in 2011 (the paper was in 2012, but the actual network was in 2011).
Implementing model parallelization by hand in 2011 was a huge feat of engineering.
Alex Krajewski was a wonderful programmer and implemented all of this by hand.
These days, we don't need to implement such things by hand.
Cloud codes do not require manual implementation of distributing weight matrices across GPUs.

In the example parallel network, the two GPUs exchange information only at two places.
AlexNet was a breakthrough in deep learning.
After AlexNet, the field of convolutional networks grew rapidly.
Convolutional networks can be improved significantly using relatively simple ideas.
The speaker previously discussed important ideas about convolutional networks with Alex Davidov.
AlexNet used 11 by 11 convolutions in its first layer.
Modern convolutional networks typically use only 3 by 3 convolutions, or occasionally 5 by 5.
The VGG idea allows representing large convolutions as compositions of smaller convolutions.
Using compositions of small convolutions reduces the number of weights compared to large convolutions.
Composing small convolutions provides additional structural regularization.
In a convolutional network, the same processing is applied to different parts of the input, which acts as a form of regularization.
This regularization typically improves network performance.
The Inception architecture was discussed with Alex Davidov.
The Inception idea is related to the concept of 'network in network'.
Earlier in the course, the speaker discussed processing image tiles with small neural networks.
In those earlier discussions, the small neural networks were extremely simple, consisting of just a single matrix multiplication.
A simple small neural network takes the flattened input, multiplies it by a weight matrix, and produces an output vector.
The Inception trick and 'network in network' ideas involve replacing the simple convolution with a more complicated network.
In the Inception approach, tiles are still processed in parallel with the same small network, but the small network is now more complex.
Inception units typically contain multiple parallel processing branches.
The presence of multiple parallel branches is intentional and will be discussed further.
The third important idea is residual connections, also associated with ResNets.
Residual connections are widely used in deep learning, including in transformers.
Residual connections were previously discussed with Alex Davidov.
In a standard feedforward network without residual connections, a layer computes f(x) from input x.
When f(x) saturates, its gradient goes to zero, preventing the layer from changing.
Without a residual connection, if a layer's gradient becomes zero, layers below it receive zero gradient and cannot learn.
A residual connection adds the input x to the output of the layer, computing f(x) + x.
With a residual connection, even if f(x) saturates and its gradient is zero, the gradient can still flow through the identity connection to lower layers.
Specifically, when the derivative of f is zero, the overall gradient through the residual block approximates the identity matrix, allowing gradients to propagate.
Kaiming He invented ResNets and called it the revolution of depth.
After the introduction of residual connections, it became possible to train convolutional networks with hundreds or thousands of layers.
AlexNet had 8 trainable layers (excluding pooling layers).
VGG had 19 trainable layers.
GoogleNet with its first inception units had 22 layers.
ResNet, introduced the next year, had about 150 layers.
With residual connections, networks with 200, 300, 500, or even 2000 layers can still be trained.
Increasing the depth of ResNets beyond a certain point does not continue to improve performance.
Adding new layers is only beneficial as long as they improve results.
Practical ResNets typically have up to about 200 layers, beyond which gains diminish.
The speaker announces that he will discuss bottleneck layers and the split-transform-merge idea.
Bottleneck layers and split-transform-merge are key ideas in convolutional architectures.
The VGG idea reduces the number of weights by replacing a large convolution with a sequence of small convolutions.
Convolutional layers inherently have far fewer weights than fully connected layers, but further reduction is possible.
It is possible to improve convolutional layers by further reducing the number of weights.
A standard convolutional layer receives a 3D input tensor of depth D, width W, and height H.
The output of a convolutional layer is a vector of features of size D'.
The weight tensor of a standard convolutional layer has dimensions D × W × H × D'.
The speaker estimates that a convolutional layer with 256 input channels, a 3x3 kernel, and 256 output channels has around 700,000 weights.
The bottleneck idea aims to reduce the number of weights in a convolutional layer.
The bottleneck idea proposes to first compress the feature depth using a 1x1 convolution before applying the spatial convolution.
In a bottleneck layer, the input first passes through a 1x1 convolution that reduces the depth to a smaller value D'' (e.g., from 256 to 32).
The 1x1 convolution does not affect spatial geometry; it only transforms the feature dimension.
After depth reduction, a spatial convolution (e.g., 3x3) is applied, operating on the reduced depth D''.
If the output depth needs to be D', another 1x1 convolution is used to expand the depth back to D'.
The first 1x1 convolution in a bottleneck has D × 1 × 1 × D'' weights.
The spatial convolution in a bottleneck has D'' × W × H × D'' weights.
The second 1x1 convolution has D'' × 1 × 1 × D' weights.
The bottleneck design avoids the large D × D' × W × H product, significantly reducing the total number of weights.
In the bottleneck, the spatial convolution multiplies the kernel size (e.g., 9) by (D'')^2 instead of D^2, where D'' is much smaller than D.
The bottleneck example uses three convolutions instead of one.
Nevertheless, a lot of weights are saved.
In the example with three convolutions, the weight count is about 256 times 100.
Without the bottleneck, the weight count is about 256 times 2,500.
The weight reduction factor is about 25 times.
In the bottleneck idea, a vector of 256 features is compressed down to 32 numbers.
Decompressing from 32 numbers back to 256 cannot restore the lost information.
Geometrically, the bottleneck operates in a high-dimensional feature space (dimension 256) and selects a specific subspace of much smaller dimension.
The process reduces long, complicated features to a much smaller dimension.
The single bottleneck is equivalent to taking just one view of the features.
If the network only needed 32 numbers, the previous layer could directly produce 32 features instead of 256, saving even more weights.
The simple bottleneck idea as initially described does not work by itself.
The simple bottleneck never appears in practice in that form.
The bottleneck becomes useful when multiple copies of the processing pipeline are used in parallel.
In practice, multiple copies of the processing pipeline are used, starting from an input tensor of size D x W x H.
With D=256, a single pipeline outputs a vector of size 32.
To reconstruct a vector of size 256, eight such pipelines are needed, and their outputs are concatenated.
Each parallel pipeline learns different weights, implementing different processing.
Using eight parallel pipelines reduces the weight savings from 25 times to about 4 times compared to the original single bottleneck.
Even with reduced savings, the parallel approach is still a good idea in practice.
In the split-transform-merge approach, multiple different projections of the high-dimensional feature space are used.
These projections correspond to different viewpoints or snapshots of the feature space.
Using multiple learned projections can lead to better performance than processing the original high-dimensional features directly.
It is often beneficial to use many random projections of high-dimensional objects.
In this architecture, the projections are learned and trained to be useful, which is better than random.
The approach is called split, transform, merge.
The split, transform, merge pattern is a standard idea in convolutional architectures.
ResNeXt provides an example of the split-transform-merge idea.
In the ResNeXt example, the 256 channels are split into 32 paths of 4 channels each.
This is an extreme projection with several extreme projections, which works better.
Inception networks and Inception ResNet networks are important classical convolutional architectures.
For a long time, they were the best available backbones for many computer vision tasks.
Object detection and segmentation architectures typically cannot be trained from scratch due to limited labeled data.
In practice, a backbone network pre-trained on ImageNet for classification is used as a feature extractor.
The classification head of the pre-trained network is removed, and the rest is used as the backbone.
The Inception ResNet family was one of the most influential backbone families around 2016.
The main idea of Inception networks is to use better basic blocks that process inputs, like small neural networks.
Progress in Inception networks came from inventing better basic blocks version after version.
In Inception networks, pooling layers were replaced with trainable blocks that can reduce dimensions.
Strided convolutions are used in these blocks to reduce the spatial geometry.
Later Inception networks had reduction blocks that may contain pooling inside.
The reduction blocks also follow the split-transform-merge idea with parallel processing lines whose results are merged.
Residual connections were added to Inception networks to create Inception ResNet.
Inception ResNet V2 was a very influential backbone that was used widely.
There are two different objectives when optimizing network architecture: memory and latency.
Reducing the number of weights reduces memory, as network size is essentially the number of weights.
Latency refers to how quickly the network runs.
Real-time applications, like surveillance camera tracking, require the network to process at least 30 frames per second, preferably 60.
A smaller network may run faster, but latency primarily depends on the number of layers.
Once the network fits in GPU memory, the main factor for latency is the number of processing steps (layers).
The number of weights per layer can affect latency, but the number of layers is the most important component.
These two objectives (memory reduction and latency reduction) do not conflict much but are distinct.
MobileNet was designed to put computer vision on mobile devices.
EfficientNet is the family of CNNs that topped the progress of CNN architectures.
EfficientNet is widely used currently.
EfficientNet's development followed a similar pattern to that of activation functions.
Gradient descent algorithms were not discussed.
In EfficientNet, the architecture was found automatically using a neural architecture search.
The researchers of EfficientNet investigated how to scale a convolutional network.
There are multiple dimensions (knobs) that can be changed when scaling a convolutional network.
One scaling dimension is depth, which is the number of layers.
Another dimension is width, which is the length of the feature vector.
Making the network wider adds more features.
Making the network wider requires more weights.
Another dimension is resolution, which refers to the number of pixels in the input.
The number of weights in the network is determined by taking the product of depth, width, and resolution and exponentiating it.
The goal of scaling is to find the perfect balance between depth, width, and resolution.
The depth grows exponentially with an exponent alpha.
The width grows exponentially with an exponent beta.
The resolution grows exponentially with an exponent gamma.
There is a natural relation between alpha, beta, and gamma.
The researchers performed a large evolutionary search to find the best values of alpha, beta, and gamma.
The researchers were successful in finding the optimal scaling hyperparameters.
The EfficientNet family achieved state-of-the-art results across the whole field.
A plot is described with the x-axis representing the number of parameters.
Having more parameters is undesirable for efficiency.
The y-axis represents ImageNet top-1 accuracy.
Higher accuracy is better.
The best networks lie in the top left corner (few parameters, high accuracy).
There is a trade-off: larger networks generally achieve higher accuracy than smaller networks.
The Pareto frontier is the set of points where for every size, the best accuracy is achieved and for every accuracy, the smallest network is used.
The EfficientNet family succeeded in defining this Pareto frontier everywhere in the plot.
Since EfficientNet, there has not been a revolution in convolutional networks.
To a large extent, the field switched from convolutional networks to transformers.
Transformers will be discussed later in the lecture.
In convolutional networks, EfficientNet is still considered the best underlying architecture.
For some object detection and segmentation pipelines, EfficientNet is used as the backbone.
Batch normalization averages the same feature over spatial dimensions and across mini-batch examples.
Layer normalization does not average over the mini-batch; it effectively uses a mini-batch size of one.
In layer normalization, averaging is done over the entire tensor of features.
Layer normalization provides global statistics for the whole layer.
Layer normalization is commonly used in transformers.
Transformers are large models that typically cannot use large mini-batches.
In transformers, normalization is performed within a single training sample.
The field of normalization techniques is large, with many papers and results.
Convolutional networks will reappear in practical sessions.
The next topic is recurrent neural networks (RNNs).
Until transformers appeared, convolutional networks and recurrent networks were the two main architecture families in deep learning.
Recurrent networks are designed for sequence data.
Input data often comes as sequences.
An image is a two-dimensional structure, not a sequence; CNNs are suited for images.
Time series data, such as financial time series, are examples of sequences.
Sound is a sequence of amplitude values over time.
In classical machine learning and digital signal processing, raw sound sequences are too long to handle directly.
To process sound, it is cut into short packets (20-30 milliseconds), and feature extraction is applied per packet, resulting in a sequence of feature vectors.
Text is a key example of sequence data.
Text is a sequence of tokens, such as words or subwords.
Text is inherently one-dimensional.
Sequence-to-single-output problems take a sequence as input and produce a single output, e.g., text classification.
Classifying news articles into topics (sports, politics, science) is an example of sequence-to-single-output.
Single-input-to-sequence problems generate a sequence from a single input, e.g., image captioning.
In image captioning, the input is an image and the output is a text sequence that describes the image.
Sequence-to-sequence problems have both input and output as sequences, e.g., machine translation.
Machine translation converts text from one language to another.
Sequence labeling problems involve input and output sequences of the same length, aligned element-wise.
Part-of-speech tagging is a sequence labeling task where each word in a sentence gets a part-of-speech tag.
Video is a sequence of frames (images).
Adding subtitles to a movie is a sequence-based task.
In object tracking, you have a video and you are supposed to follow an object inside the video.
Object tracking involves segmentation on a sequence of images to track the same object as it moves.
Convolutional networks are not well suited for dealing with sequences.
A sliding window can be used along an input sequence to process parts of the sequence.
There was a time when convolutional approaches were rivals to recurrent approaches in natural language processing.
Transformers changed the landscape of natural language processing.
The most important thing for sequence processing is to have a way to recall inputs from long ago.
Understanding a whole sentence requires recalling what happened at the beginning.
Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) process sequences by updating a hidden state.
An RNN has inputs x1, x2, ..., xt.
Each input in the sequence is processed separately by a recurrent unit.
A recurrent unit takes two inputs: the current input x and a hidden state h.
A recurrent unit outputs an updated hidden state h' and optionally an output.
The hidden state h is assumed to capture the previous part of the sequence (before x).
A recurrent unit is a function f(x, h) that outputs h'.
In an RNN, the hidden state is a vector of numbers that goes along the network and is updated with each new input.
In an RNN, the hidden state combines all relevant information from the sequence so far.
The hidden state is initialized with some H0.
The recurrent network produces outputs H1, H2, ..., Ht, Ht+1, ...
A standard recurrent network uses shared weights across all recurrent cells.

In classical recurrent networks, a recurrent cell performs linear transformations: x multiplied by matrix A, h multiplied by matrix B, then the results are added and passed through an activation function G.
The update formula for a classical recurrent cell is h' = G(A * x + B * h), where G is an activation function such as hyperbolic tangent or ELU, and A and B are weight matrices.
Recurrent networks have been around since the second half of the 1980s.
Training recurrent networks was difficult due to limited compute at the time.
A unidirectional RNN processes input in only one direction, for example left to right.
For classification based on the last hidden state, reading left to right or right to left is acceptable.
For sequence labeling tasks such as part-of-speech tagging, a unidirectional RNN only allows looking at previous words, which is problematic.
Bidirectional RNNs have two RNNs: one left-to-right and one right-to-left.
In a bidirectional RNN, at time t, the left-to-right part captures left context and the right-to-left part captures right context.
In a bidirectional RNN, a classification head can merge the results from both directions to output yt, accounting for both left and right context.
Bidirectional RNNs should be used unless the problem prohibits it, such as in language modeling where only left context is available.
In language modeling, predicting the next word is based only on the left context.
In real-time object tracking, the video stream does not allow access to future frames far ahead, so one-sided networks are needed.
In many sequence-to-sequence problems, the whole input can be read before making a decision, so bidirectional RNNs are applicable.
In a unidirectional RNN with shared weights, the same weight matrix W participates in every recurrent cell.
Training separate matrices for each time step is infeasible.
In a unidirectional RNN for sequence classification, the whole sequence is read and then classified using a head and a loss function.
The loss function compares the predicted answer with the correct answer.
In an RNN, the output can be produced at every cell, or only from the last hidden state using a head, depending on the problem.
The described recurrent neural network method can process arbitrary sequences of arbitrary length.
The same weight matrix W is used for all time steps in this method.
Using the same weight matrix W across all time steps leads to problems with gradient flow.
Gradients of the loss function flow backward through the network along the sequence during training.
The gradient of the loss with respect to a specific weight w is a sum of contributions from each time step because the same weight is used repeatedly.
The repeated use of the same weight matrix W is similar to weight sharing in convolutional networks.
In convolutional networks, the same weight is used across different spatial locations, enabling parallel processing across the whole image.
Weight sharing allows sparse activations and sparse gradients, but the gradients accumulate over the shared weights, so it is not a problem.
In recurrent networks, every weight is very important because of the accumulation effect of repeated use.
In a simplified recurrent network model without activation functions or inputs, each hidden state H_t is obtained by multiplying the previous hidden state H_{t-1} by the weight matrix W.
In the simplified model, H1 equals W times H0.
In the simplified model, H2 equals W times H1, which equals W squared times H0.
In the simplified model, H_T equals W to the power T times H0.
Matrices have a property called the spectral radius.
The spectral radius indicates how the matrix scales the length of a vector when multiplied.
The norm of h_t is approximately the spectral radius of W times the norm of h_{t-1}.
After t applications, the norm of h_t is approximately (spectral radius)^t times the norm of h_0.
If the spectral radius of W is greater than 1, the activations explode.
Even a spectral radius slightly above 1 (e.g., 1.1 or 1.05) causes exponential growth over long sequences.
Exploding activations can cause numerical overflows.
Huge activations do not reflect meaningful computations.
The same issue occurs in the backward pass because gradients involve multiplications by W (or its transpose).
There are two types of gradient problems: exploding gradients and vanishing gradients.
Exploding gradients occur when the spectral radius is greater than 1, causing gradients to grow to infinity.
Vanishing gradients occur when the spectral radius is less than 1, causing gradients to shrink to zero.
In the case of vanishing gradients, gradients for early sequence elements exponentially decay to zero.
Vanishing gradients prevent the network from learning long-term dependencies, effectively limiting long-term memory.
The influence of earlier parts of the sequence vanishes quickly due to vanishing gradients.
Exploding gradients cause the training to break (e.g., numerical issues).
Vanishing gradients do not cause numerical failure but prevent effective learning.
The solution to exploding gradients is gradient clipping.
Gradient clipping involves capping the norm of the gradient vector (e.g., projecting back to a unit sphere if it exceeds a threshold).
Gradient clipping is applied repeatedly during training whenever the gradient norm becomes too large.
Gradient clipping is a simple approach; it does not require constraining the spectral radius to exactly 1.
Both Keras and PyTorch support gradient clipping.
There is a paper from 2013 by Pascanu that studied the behavior of recurrent networks.
The Pascanu paper contains interesting points about the training dynamics of recurrent networks.
The paper is recommended for reading.
The paper is not about new architectures or improving performance, but about understanding the space of activations and weights during training.
An exploding gradient corresponds to a loss surface that has a region of normal gradients and then a steep wall where the loss increases extremely rapidly, causing huge gradients.
Without gradient clipping, optimization would fly away to poor regions after hitting the steep wall.
With gradient clipping, after hitting the steep wall, the update direction is projected back to a normal regime, and optimization continues in approximately the desired direction.
Clipping gradients is an acceptable transformation that does not harm the optimization direction.
In recurrent neural networks, both activations and gradients can blow up or vanish.
It is difficult to make the spectral radius exactly 1.
Solving the exploding gradients problem is easy (via clipping).
Solving the vanishing gradients problem is more difficult and will be discussed later.

Practical sessions with Alex are on Thursday.
There will be a midterm presentation on Friday.

The list of papers should be made available today.
On Friday, students will present.

summary.text: AlexNet, introduced by Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Hinton in 2012, was the first convolutional network to decisively beat classical computer vision methods on ImageNet.
AlexNet cut the ImageNet error rate from about 22–23% down to 13%.
The improvement by AlexNet was so large that the next year's ImageNet leaderboard consisted entirely of convolutional networks.
AlexNet introduced the first industrial-scale instance of model parallelization.
The AlexNet model was too large for a single GPU.
AlexNet was split into two pipelines that exchanged information only at a couple of points.
Model parallelization remains the key idea when a network does not fit on one GPU.
In model parallelization, different weight tensors are placed on different devices.
PyTorch handles the communication automatically in model parallelization.
Data parallelization distributes different mini-batch examples to different GPUs.
Data parallelization averages the weight updates from different GPUs.
Data parallelization scales the mini-batch size without changing the model.
The VGG network established that a stack of several 3x3 convolutions can replace one large convolution.
A 3x3 convolution looks at a small neighbourhood.
Stacking two 3x3 convolutional layers gives an effective receptive field of 5x5.
Stacking three 3x3 convolutional layers gives an effective receptive field of 7x7.
A stack of 3x3 convolutions has dramatically fewer weights than a single large filter with the same receptive field.
The extra depth from stacking 3x3 convolutions acts as an additional structural regularisation.
The extra depth forces the network to process the input in the same way across different locations.
Modern specialised GPU primitives are heavily optimised for 3x3 convolutions.
This GPU optimisation makes the VGG design of stacking 3x3 convolutions even more practical.
An Inception unit runs several parallel convolutional operations (1x1, 3x3, 5x5) and pooling, and concatenates their outputs.
An Inception unit treats each spatial tile with a small custom network rather than a single linear filter.
Inception v2 and v3 further factorise large filters by replacing an n x n convolution with a sequence of n x 1 and 1 x n convolutions, saving even more parameters.

Inception v3 introduced label smoothing, which trains the network with a target distribution q'(k) = (1 - ε)[k=y] + ε u(k), where u(k) is a prior (usually uniform), instead of the hard one-hot target q(k)=[k=y].
Label smoothing prevents the softmax arguments from growing unboundedly and reduces overconfidence.
A deep plain network (without skip connections) suffers from vanishing gradients.
In a deep plain network, when a layer saturates, its derivative becomes tiny, cutting off gradient flow to all earlier layers.
ResNet solves the vanishing gradient problem with a skip-connection that computes the output as y^(k) = F(x^(k)) + x^(k).
The ResNet skip-connection makes the gradient ∂y^(k)/∂x^(k) = 1 + ∂F(x^(k))/∂x^(k), so even when F saturates, the gradient still propagates.
Kaiming He called the ResNet skip-connection the 'revolution of depth'.
The ResNet skip-connection allowed networks with 150, 200, or more layers to train reliably.
ResNets stop improving beyond about 200 layers, but they do not break (training remains stable).
Highway networks use an output that is a convex combination of the input and the transformed signal: y^(k) = C(x^(k)) x^(k) + T(x^(k)) F(x^(k)), where C = 1 - T.
Empirical evidence shows that keeping the residual path as straightforward as possible (just addition without gating) works best.
A typical convolutional layer with D=256 input channels, D'=256 output channels, and 3x3 filters has about 590,000 parameters.

A bottleneck layer reduces parameter count by projecting to a smaller number of channels with a 1x1 convolution, performing the spatial convolution in that low-dimensional space, and then projecting back with another 1x1 convolution.
A single bottleneck that compresses a rich feature vector (e.g., 256 channels) to a much smaller number (e.g., 32) loses information that the final expansion cannot recover.
If only 32 features were needed, the previous layer could directly produce 32 channels, making a bottleneck unnecessary.
A bottleneck makes sense only when replicated several times in parallel.
The split-transform-merge paradigm consists of splitting input channels into groups, transforming each group independently, and merging the results (typically by concatenation).
For D=256, using eight parallel pathways that each reduce to 32 channels and then concatenate back to 256 replaces one large weight tensor with eight small ones.
In the described parallel split, the weight saving is roughly 4×, compared to a single bottleneck's saving of 25×, and this saving is still substantial.
Each parallel pathway in the split-transform-merge approach learns a different projection onto a low-dimensional subspace.
The network captures several distinct views of the high-dimensional feature space through parallel pathways.
Learning multiple complementary projections often works better than processing the whole feature vector directly.
Random projections can also be helpful.
In the split-transform-merge approach, the projections are learned and task-driven.
ResNeXt uses the split-transform-merge pattern, replacing a ResNet block with parallel convolutional paths (group convolutions) whose outputs are summed.
The split-transform-merge pattern is a direct descendant of the Inception unit.
The split-transform-merge pattern is closely related to group convolutions.
Group convolutions were first used in AlexNet for parallelisation across GPUs.
In group convolutions, different groups naturally tend to specialise in different types of features.
Later Inception networks (v4 and Inception-ResNet) further simplified and standardised the building blocks.
Inception v4 introduced a uniform stem, three basic block types (A, B, C), and dedicated reduction blocks that halve spatial dimensions using strided convolutions and occasional pooling.
The reduction blocks in Inception v4 learn how to downsample, instead of using a fixed pooling layer.
Inception-ResNet added residual connections inside Inception blocks, resulting in state-of-the-art backbones around 2016.
Inception-ResNet-v2 was especially influential.

For downstream tasks with scarce labelled data, the standard approach is to use a network pre-trained on ImageNet with its classification head removed as a fixed or fine-tuned feature extractor (backbone).
Inception-ResNet models served as highly effective backbones for years.
For practical deployment, memory (total number of parameters) is an important resource, and a smaller footprint is essential for mobile or embedded devices.
Latency (forward pass time) is another important resource for practical deployment.
Latency depends primarily on the number of layers (sequential steps).
Latency depends secondarily on layer sizes, once the model fits on the accelerator.
SqueezeNet uses fire modules, each composed of a squeeze layer (1x1 convolutions that reduce channel count) and an expand layer (a mix of 1x1 and 3x3 convolutions).
SqueezeNet delays spatial downsampling as long as possible to keep activation maps large, helping accuracy despite parameter reduction.
SqueezeNet achieves 50 times fewer parameters than AlexNet at comparable accuracy.
MobileNet focuses on latency-sensitive mobile applications.
MobileNet uses depthwise separable convolutions, which factorise a standard convolution into a depthwise convolution (one filter per input channel) and a pointwise 1x1 convolution.
Depthwise separable convolutions provide enormous savings in parameters and FLOPs, with only a small drop in accuracy.
EfficientNet was discovered by neural architecture search in 2019 by Tan and Le.
EfficientNet's key insight is compound scaling, where a convolutional network is scaled along depth (number of layers), width (channel count), and resolution (input pixel count).
In EfficientNet's compound scaling, if depth scales by α^φ, width by β^φ, resolution by γ^φ, then total parameter count scales approximately as (α·β·γ)^φ.
EfficientNet uses an evolutionary search to find optimal α, β, γ for a base model, then scales the model with a single compound coefficient φ.
The EfficientNet family defines the Pareto frontier on accuracy versus parameter plots, providing the best accuracy for a given size and the smallest network for a given accuracy.
EfficientNet remains the dominant CNN backbone for many tasks, even as transformers have become popular in other areas.
During training, each layer’s weight update changes the distribution of its outputs, forcing the next layer to re-adapt.
Internal covariate shift slows down learning and can drive neurons into saturated regimes.
Naive normalisation of layer outputs using the full dataset or full whitening is computationally prohibitive and interferes with gradient updates (e.g., bias can diverge).
Batch normalisation (BN) normalises each feature over the current mini-batch using x̂_k = (x_k - E[x_k])/√Var[x_k], where the statistics are computed on the mini-batch.
To prevent loss of non-linearity, BN introduces learnable scale γ_k and shift β_k to compute y_k = γ_k x̂_k + β_k.
When γ_k = √Var[x_k] and β_k = E[x_k], the BN layer can pass the input through unchanged.
Although originally motivated by reducing internal covariate shift, later studies showed that BN's benefits do not come from that.
BN smooths the loss landscape (reducing Lipschitz constant), decouples direction and length of weight vectors, and often leads to linear convergence of gradient descent.
In practice, BN acts as a regulariser, making dropout unnecessary.
All modern normalisation methods share the same core operations but differ in the dimensions over which statistics are computed.
Batch Normalization normalises over the batch and spatial dimensions (N, H, W) for each channel, and is standard for CNNs.
Layer Normalization normalises over all channels and spatial dimensions (C, H, W) per sample, with no mini-batch dependency, and is used extensively in transformers.
Instance Normalization normalises over spatial dimensions (H, W) per sample and per channel, and is used in style transfer (e.g., AdaIN).
Group Normalization splits channels into groups and normalises over each group's spatial dimensions, and is used with weight standardisation in Big Transfer (BiT).
Weight Standardisation normalises the weights themselves channel-wise, smoothing gradients during backpropagation.
The choice of normalisation method is largely dictated by the architecture and effective batch size.
Many real-world inputs are inherently sequential, such as financial time series, sound, video, and text (a sequence of tokens).
In many-to-one problems, a sequence input produces a single output, such as in text classification or sentiment analysis.
In one-to-many problems, a single input produces a sequence, such as in image captioning.
In sequence-to-sequence problems, both input and output are sequences of possibly different lengths, such as in machine translation.
In sequence labelling problems, input and output are aligned sequences of the same length, such as part-of-speech tagging or frame-wise video annotation.
A sliding-window convolutional approach can handle sequences to some extent, but lacks a mechanism to remember tokens far from the current window.
Understanding a paragraph requires holding information from its beginning.
An RNN processes a sequence one element at a time while maintaining a hidden state vector h_t.
The hidden state is updated recursively as h_t = f(x_t, h_{t-1}).
The same function f and weight matrices are reused for every time step in an RNN.
Recurrent weight sharing allows RNNs to handle sequences of arbitrary length.
In RNNs, every time step contributes to the gradient of the shared weights, analogous to how a convolutional filter receives gradients from all spatial positions.
The simplest recurrent cell is a linear map followed by a non-linearity.
In the simplest recurrent cell, $a_t = b + W h_{t-1} + U x_t$.
The hidden state update is $h_t = \phi(a_t)$.
$\phi$ is typically $\tanh$ or a similar saturating activation function.
An output $y_t$ can be produced at every time step or only after the last hidden state, depending on the task.
A single-direction RNN only sees the past context.
For tasks such as sequence labelling, the prediction at position $t$ should ideally use both left and right context.
A bidirectional RNN runs two independent networks: one that processes the sequence left-to-right and one that processes right-to-left.
At each step, the bidirectional RNN concatenates (or otherwise merges) the hidden states from the two directions.
Concatenating the hidden states gives the predictor access to the full surrounding context.
The exception is tasks where future information is genuinely unavailable.
Language modelling (predicting the next word) is an example of such an exceptional task.
Online object tracking is another example of such an exceptional task.
These exceptional tasks must process a live stream without look-ahead.
Training an RNN means computing the gradient of a loss $L$ with respect to the shared weight matrices.
The loss $L$ can be defined on the final output or on each step.
The computational graph is an unrolled chain.
At each time step, the same weight matrix $W$ participates both in the forward computation and in the loss.
Consequently, the total gradient is a sum over all times: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial W} = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{\partial L}{\partial h_t} \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial W}$.
The total gradient being a sum over all timesteps is the same effect that makes weight sharing effective, because every timestep provides a signal, but it also introduces a serious difficulty.
Consider a drastically simplified recurrence where $h_t = W h_{t-1}$, ignoring inputs and non-linearities.
In this simplified recurrence, $h_T = W^{\,T} h_0$.
The norm of $h_T$ behaves like $(\rho)^T \|h_0\|$, where $\rho$ is the spectral radius of $W$.
The spectral radius of $W$ is roughly the factor by which multiplying by $W$ scales a vector.
The same repeated multiplication occurs during the backward pass because gradients flow through the transpose.
If $\rho > 1$, the activations and gradients explode exponentially.
Exploding gradients lead to numerical overflow, chaotic loss surfaces, and non-sensical updates.
If $\rho < 1$, the signals vanish exponentially.
Vanishing gradients cause the network to become unable to learn long-range dependencies: the influence of early tokens on the loss quickly approaches zero.
Both exploding and vanishing gradient regimes are common in practice.
It is very difficult to keep the spectral radius $\rho$ precisely at $1$ throughout training.
The exploding gradient problem has an elegantly simple solution: gradient clipping.
In gradient clipping, whenever the norm of a gradient exceeds a predefined threshold, the vector is rescaled to that threshold.
There are two common variants of gradient clipping: clipping by norm and clipping by component value.
In Keras, an example of clipping by norm is `optimizers.SGD(lr=0.01, clipnorm=1.)`.
In Keras, an example of clipping by component value is `optimizers.SGD(lr=0.01, clipvalue=.05)`.
Geometrically, exploding gradients correspond to a near-vertical "wall" in the loss landscape.
Without gradient clipping, an optimiser would bounce off this wall and fly far away.
Gradient clipping projects the step back, keeping the search in the well-behaved region and preserving the general direction of the update.
Gradient clipping is a standard, harmless component of RNN training.
Solving the vanishing gradient problem is more subtle than solving the exploding gradient problem.
Solving the vanishing gradient problem requires carefully designed recurrent units with built-in gradient highways.
This topic leads directly to LSTM and GRU architectures.
LSTM and GRU architectures are to be discussed next.
